faqs.q: How do I convert my hourly rate to annual salary?
faqs.a: Multiply your hourly rate by hours per week (usually 38 for full-time) and then by 52 weeks. For example, $30/hour × 38 × 52 = $59,280 gross per year. This assumes no unpaid overtime or penalty rates.

faqs.q: What is the difference between the National Minimum Wage and an award rate?

faqs.q: How is superannuation calculated on top of my salary?

bodyMarkdown:
## Converting Your Hourly Rate to Annual Pay

To turn an hourly rate into an annual salary, use the standard formula: **hourly rate × hours per week × 52 weeks**. This calculation assumes you work the same number of hours every week, with no unpaid overtime, penalty rates, allowances, or salary sacrifice. For full-time employees, the typical benchmark is 38 hours per week, as set by the Fair Work Ombudsman. If your hours differ, adjust accordingly.

For example, an hourly rate of $30.00 gives:
- Weekly: $30.00 × 38 = $1,140.00
- Annual: $1,140.00 × 52 = $59,280.00

You can use [the timesheet](/) to enter your base hourly rate and see the annual, monthly, fortnightly, and weekly figures instantly. The timesheet includes a checkbox to add 25% casual loading on top of your base rate – never enter a rate that already includes casual loading.

## National Minimum Wage vs Award Rates

The **National Minimum Wage** (NMW) is the legal minimum for employees not covered by an award or registered agreement. From 1 July 2026, the NMW is **$26.44 per hour**, or **$1,004.90 per week** for a 38-hour week. Casual employees receive an additional 25% loading, bringing the casual rate to **$33.05 per hour**.

However, most Australian workers are covered by an **award** – an industry or occupation-specific minimum set by the Fair Work Commission. Award rates are almost always higher than the NMW. For example, a retail employee or hospitality worker may be entitled to a higher base rate plus penalty rates for weekends or late nights. To find the correct minimum for your job, check the relevant [pay guides](/blog) on the Fair Work Ombudsman website.

### The Average Salary in China in Context

When discussing global pay comparisons, the **average salary in China** often comes up as a benchmark for emerging economies. According to the Australian Bureau of Statistics, the average full-time adult ordinary time earnings in Australia (May 2026) were **$2,083.70 per week**, or about **$108,352 per year**. This is an average across all industries and states, not a median for any specific job. By contrast, the average salary in China varies widely by region and industry, but it remains significantly lower than Australian averages when converted to Australian dollars. Australia’s National Minimum Wage alone provides a baseline that exceeds many global averages, highlighting the strength of our labour protections.

## Fortnightly Pay and Budgeting

Many Australian employers pay fortnightly. To find your fortnightly gross pay, simply double your weekly figure. For the NMW:
- Weekly: $1,004.90
- Fortnightly: $2,009.80

Knowing your fortnightly amount helps with budgeting for bills, rent, and savings. The [reference tables](/data) on this site include common conversions for various hourly rates.

## Tax and Superannuation

Your annual gross pay is not what you take home. The Australian Taxation Office applies the 2026–27 resident tax rates:
- Nil tax on the first $18,200
- 15% on income from $18,201 to $45,000
- 30% on income from $45,001 to $135,000
- 37% on income from $135,001 to $190,000
- 45% on income above $190,000

Plus the **Medicare levy** of 2% (using the 2025–26 single reduction thresholds as 2026–27 thresholds were not confirmed). For a full-time NMW earner ($52,265 annual), the estimated tax and Medicare would be approximately $6,800, leaving about $45,465 take-home pay.

**Superannuation** is paid on top of your gross salary by your employer. The super guarantee rate is **12% of ordinary earnings**, up to the maximum contribution base of **$270,830** per year. For the NMW example, that’s an extra $6,272 into your super fund annually. Super is not deducted from your pay; it’s an additional benefit.

## Using the Timesheet and Other Resources

To get a personalised estimate, use [the timesheet](/) on this site. Enter your base hourly rate, and the calculator will show annual, monthly, fortnightly, and weekly figures. If you are a casual employee, tick the casual loading checkbox – the calculator will add 25% to your base rate automatically. Remember, the result is an estimate: it assumes the same rate every week, no unpaid overtime, no penalty rates, no allowances, and no salary sacrifice. Super is estimated at 12% of ordinary earnings only, paid on top, and stops at the $270,830 maximum contribution base. Tax uses the 2026–27 resident scale with the full tax-free threshold. HELP, the Medicare levy surcharge, and salary packaging are not deducted.

For more detailed information, explore the [minimum wage](/topics/minimum-wage) page, [take-home pay](/topics/take-home) guide, or [super and packaging](/topics/super-and-packaging) topic. If you want to compare your rate to industry averages, the [average pay](/topics/average-pay) page provides ABS data – but remember these are averages, not medians for your specific job.

Understanding the difference between the National Minimum Wage and award rates is crucial. While the NMW is the floor, your actual entitlement may be higher. Always check your award or enterprise agreement. The Fair Work Ombudsman’s pay guides are the authoritative source.

Whether you are negotiating a salary, planning your budget, or simply curious, converting your hourly rate to annual pay gives you a clearer picture of your earnings. And when you hear discussions about the **average salary in China** or other global benchmarks, remember that Australia’s minimum wage and superannuation system provide a strong foundation for workers.
